title: Hash-based indexing
lead: Static hashing, collisions, extendible hashing and directory growth.

sections.title: Hashing and equality lookup
sections.html:
A hash function maps a search key to a bucket. Equal keys map to the same bucket, but different keys can collide, so actual keys must still be compared. Chaining and open addressing are common in-memory collision strategies.

Database hash indexes organise entries in page-sized buckets. They support equality predicates; hash order does not preserve key order and therefore does not locate an arbitrary key range efficiently. Hashing is also used for joins, grouping and duplicate elimination.

Static hashing fixes the primary bucket count. Dynamic hashing adjusts the structure as entries are inserted. The source develops extendible hashing; linear hashing is listed but not developed.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Static chained hashing
sections.html:
Static chained hashing allocates N primary bucket pages. The hash function has range 0 through N − 1. A full bucket uses linked overflow pages. Search follows its bucket chain; insertion and deletion modify the appropriate page.

Without overflow, locating a bucket entry needs approximately one page read, while a modification additionally writes its page. These costs concern index entries; by-reference indexes may also need data-page fetches.

A good hash function distributes keys across buckets, but skew and growth can still create long chains. Shrinking data can leave mostly empty buckets. Rehashing restores distribution at the cost of reading and rebuilding the index.

PDF pp. 7–12

sections.title: Extendible hashing and depth
sections.html:
Extendible hashing uses a directory of bucket pointers. With global depth g, the directory has 2g entries, selected using g hash bits. The source uses least-significant bits.

Each bucket has local depth d, the number of hash bits shared by its entries. If d < g, multiple directory entries point to that bucket. Lookup follows the directory pointer and compares actual keys within the bucket.

Insertion into a bucket with room changes no directory structure. When the bucket is full, the system splits that bucket and redistributes its entries using one more hash bit. Most other buckets remain untouched.

PDF pp. 13–20

sections.title: Bucket splits and directory doubling
sections.html:
If a full bucket has d < g, increase its local depth, split it and update the relevant directory pointers. The existing directory already distinguishes the extra bit, so its size is unchanged.

If d = g, the split requires an additional directory bit. Double the directory, increase global depth and redirect pointers for the two split buckets. Entries are redistributed only for the bucket being split. Repeated splits may be necessary if the new bit still fails to separate the keys.

The source insertion sequence grows global depth from 2 to 3. Directory growth is cheaper than redistributing every data page, but directory size and hash skew remain practical constraints.

PDF pp. 21–26

quiz.question: A bucket with local depth 2 and global depth 4 is split into buckets with local depth 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The directory does not need to double
quiz.explanation: Before the split the directory uses four bits. The split only needs three bits to distinguish the two new buckets, so the existing directory is already sufficient. The old bucket has 2^(4−2)=4 pointers; after redirection each new depth-three bucket has 2^(4−3)=2. Other buckets need not split.
